paragraphs.heading: What apologetics means
paragraphs.text: Are there answers to our questions? From the simplest things that pass through our consciousness to the big questions about life and faith. The word apologetics comes from the Greek word apologia, which can be translated as answer. It means to give a reason, a defense, or an answer for what we believe and why we believe it.

paragraphs.heading: A flight home from a wedding
paragraphs.text: When I was in college, I went to a friend's wedding and had to fly home alone. I got to the airport in the morning and learned that my flight was delayed about three or four hours, so I turned around to go wait. I saw another young man about my age. He was in college, and I thought, here's an opportunity to go talk with him and maybe share my faith. But then my next thought was, I am really tired. God, if you want me to share with him, he's going to have to sit by me on the plane.

I finally boarded the plane and sat down in seat 9A. A few moments later, I saw this young man walking down the aisle, and of course I'm wondering where he's going to sit. He sits right next to me in 9B. Whether this was a sign from God or not, it certainly was an opportunity, so I introduced myself, struck up a conversation, and eventually the topic turned toward spiritual things. He asked me what I believe.

I said, I'm a Christian, I believe in Jesus. He said, if you're a Christian, does that mean you think that the Bible is true and it's the Word of God? I said, yes. He looked at me point blank, and I'll never forget it. He said, how do you really know the Bible's true? Although my parents had trained me to give an answer, for some reason in this circumstance I fumbled around, and to be honest with you, I gave an answer that was really weak.

paragraphs.heading: A resolve to have a reason
paragraphs.text: I walked away from that encounter a little bit upset and frustrated that I didn't have a better response. I remember thinking, next time, I'm going to have a better answer. In fact, I remember having a resolve that said, if God gives me the chance to be in significant spiritual conversations again, I'm going to have a good reason for why I believe in Christianity, and specifically why I think the Bible is true.

paragraphs.heading: Christ first, then an answer
paragraphs.text: In 1 Peter 3:15, the Apostle Peter says to put Christ first in our life, but then to be ready with an answer for the hope within, and to give it with gentleness and to give it with respect toward other people. What's fascinating to me about this passage is the pattern in which Peter says to first make Christ Lord of your life, and then be ready with an answer.

Sometimes we flip this around. Sometimes we want to be ready with an answer before we've really submitted our lives to Christ, and when that happens, oftentimes the results can be harmful. But when we first find our identity in Christ and we experience his forgiveness, and then we do apologetics out of a spirit of love, it can make a powerful difference in somebody's life.

paragraphs.heading: Every Christian is an apologist
paragraphs.text: Being an apologist is not a spiritual gift like wisdom, discernment, or teaching. Being an apologist is not just for pastors, teachers, parents, and professors. We are all called to be ready with an answer for the hope within. I think C.S. Lewis is right. The question is not if we will be apologists, but how good of an apologist each of us will be.

paragraphs.heading: A staple since the beginning
paragraphs.text: Apologetics has been a staple of the Christian faith since its inception. Jesus was a kind of apologist, and of the first followers of Jesus that came after the apostles, many of them were called apologists, because they gave positive evidences for the Christian faith and responded to objections against it.

paragraphs.heading: Questions worth thinking through
paragraphs.text: How much have you thought about why you believe as you believe? Are you ready with an answer when someone asks you why you think the Bible is true? Have you thought through why, if God is all good and all powerful, he allows evil? And have you thought through a response when people say that science conflicts with faith?

And just as importantly, are you ready to share that answer with others when they ask you the reason for the hope within? We are called as Christians to be ready to make a case for the Christian faith. We're called to put forth arguments for what we believe. Now, don't confuse that with being argumentative; that's a very different thing. We are not called to be divisive in how we treat people, but each of us is called to be ready with an answer for the hope within, and that's exactly what we're going to do in this Bible study.

paragraphs.heading: Truth spoken in love
paragraphs.text: I'm going to help you develop your convictions that Christianity is true, and also have the confidence to share that faith with others. And just remember this: we are called to boldly speak truth, but we are to always do it in love.

paragraphs.heading: A day in a blindfold
paragraphs.text: In college, I had a chance to be a resident assistant, a rep in charge of fun activities and events on a floor. To help us have some compassion and understanding for students on our floor who might have handicaps, the leadership decided that we would go around for a day with a handicap of sorts. My handicap was to wear a blindfold.

It really dawned on me for the first time, since I had to go to the cafeteria and I had to go to class with this blindfold on, how tough it is to navigate life without sight. How did I cope? How did I make it through the day? I had to ask somebody to help me. Who did I ask? I didn't ask a stranger. I didn't ask somebody I just met. I asked somebody I trusted, one of my basketball teammates, to help me out through the day.

paragraphs.heading: Faith is not blind
paragraphs.text: People often have the idea that faith is blind, and that when it comes to issues of religion, it's like we're frolicking around in the dark and basing our beliefs on sheer ignorance. This might be true for some religions, but it is not true for Christianity. You see, biblically, faith is trusting what we have reason to believe is true. Just as I followed the guidance of my friend whom I had good reason to trust when I was blindfolded, God asks us to follow him, and he's given us good reasons to trust him. We are not called to blind faith.

paragraphs.heading: Miracle, knowledge, belief
paragraphs.text: We see a remarkable pattern in Exodus chapter 7 through 14. God would do a powerful miracle through Moses, a sign which gave the people knowledge of who God is, and as a result, he called them to believe in him and to place their trust in him. So here's the pattern. God would do a miracle through Moses. This gave the people knowledge, and then they were called to belief. Miracle, knowledge, belief.

Consider an example. In Exodus chapter 7 verse 17, Moses is about to do the miracle of turning the water, the Nile, into blood, and it says, by this you shall know. Now, what is this? This is the miracle Moses was about to do. And it says, and you shall know, because that miracle would give them knowledge. So Moses is doing this powerful miracle, it gives them knowledge that the God of Israel is the one true God, and then they're called to belief. So our pattern, which is clearly emerging, is miracle, knowledge, and then belief.

paragraphs.heading: The paralytic in Capernaum
paragraphs.text: We see the same pattern in the New Testament. In the Gospel of Mark, Jesus is in Capernaum and he's preaching in a home, and four men bring a paralytic to him. They can't get in to him, so they go up on the roof, remove the roof, and lower this paralytic down to Jesus. Jesus sees them, and as a result of their faith says, son, your sins are forgiven. Now the scribes and Pharisees are thinking, wait a minute, who can forgive sins but God alone? This is blasphemy.

What does Jesus do? If you skip down and look at verse 10, it says this. Jesus said, so that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins, he looked at the paralytic and said, rise, pick up your mat, and go home. Jesus did that sign as proof that gave them knowledge of who he was, and the implication was, Jesus is the Son of God, now believe in him.

paragraphs.heading: Why did they come to Jesus?
paragraphs.text: You might be thinking, wait a minute, didn't Jesus do the miracle because of the man's faith? After all, it says in Mark chapter 2 that Jesus, seeing their faith, pronounced to the man, son, your sins are forgiven. Now, it is true that God often does reward our faith by performing miracles. But let's ask a more basic question. Why did these four men and the paralytic come to Jesus in the first place? The answer is because, as Mark 1 tells us, Jesus had already been performing miracles. Jesus had already been casting out demons. He had given them evidence and signs that he's the Son of God, so they came to him with confidence and put a faith in him that was well placed.

paragraphs.heading: Come, let us reason together
paragraphs.text: Jesus calls people to love God with their heart, with their soul, with their strength, and with their minds. In the Old Testament, God says through the prophet Isaiah, come let us reason together. In the Old Testament and in the New Testament, God calls people to an intelligent faith, and he still does the same today.

paragraphs.heading: Why John recorded the signs
paragraphs.text: This is why in the Gospel of John, a gospel which is written recording the miracles of Jesus and inviting people to a confident faith, at the very end of the gospel John writes, in chapter 20 verses 30 through 31, that Jesus performed many other miracles not even recorded in this book. But they've been recorded so we might have confidence that Jesus is the Son of God, he's the Christ, and that by believing in him we may experience eternal life. The Gospel of John is written so we understand who Jesus is based on the miracles, so we can have a confident faith, and by having that faith experience eternal life.

paragraphs.heading: Investigate the evidence
paragraphs.text: Biblical faith is not blind. The Bible invites non-believers to investigate the evidence, to consider the claims of Christ, and then to consider believing in him. And as Christians, we're also not called to a blind faith. We are called to think deeply about our faith, to know why we believe what we believe. We are called to have an answer when people ask us the reason for the hope we have within.

paragraphs.heading: What Jesus actually said
paragraphs.text: Two thousand years ago, Jesus said, I'm one of the ways, one of the truths, and one possible life. If you want to come to the mother or the father through me, that's cool. Go forth living according to whatever feels right to you. Okay, you got me. Clearly, Jesus didn't say that. In fact, he said quite the opposite. If you look in the New Testament, you will find at least 100 verses that make it clear that Jesus is the only way to God, the only way to experience an eternal relationship with the Father.

paragraphs.heading: Truth matches reality
paragraphs.text: Truth is vitally important because eternity is at stake. Now, philosophers use a term that seems fancy, but I think you'll find it's kind of common sense. It's called the correspondence theory of truth. All this means is that you have a belief, an idea you hold about the world, and then you have the world over here, which is reality. Truth is not a belief. Truth is not reality. Truth is when your belief matches up with reality. That's what we mean by true. Have you ever noticed how much you base your entire life, down to the details, the daily decisions, on what you think is true?

paragraphs.heading: Is it cold outside?
paragraphs.text: What if somebody says it's cold outside? How do you check whether that is true or whether that's false? You can look at a weather app and see what information it gives you, or you could actually walk outside and see it for yourself. If it is cold outside, then your belief is true. If it's not cold outside, then the belief is false.

We do this with historical issues, such as the claim that Jesus rose from the grave, and we do this with scientific matters, such as the claim or the belief that the universe had a beginning. We actually do this on all sorts of issues. We hold a variety of beliefs, and then we go see if the world is the way we take it to be. If our beliefs match up, it's true. If our beliefs don't, it's false. But remember to keep this in mind: our beliefs don't create reality, but rather our beliefs should reflect reality.

paragraphs.heading: True for you, true for me?
paragraphs.text: You might be thinking, wait a minute, when it comes to religious claims, can't you have your beliefs and I have mine? Aren't your beliefs true for you, but my religious beliefs true for me? Not too long ago, my father was speaking at a leadership event for about 400 high school students, and in his session my dad decided to walk out into the audience and interact with the students. He started by asking a simple question to a student that was there. He said, do you think the Bible is true? The student jumped in. He goes, yes, I think the Bible's true.

My dad said, you think it's scientifically and historically accurate in everything it teaches that we properly understand? The student looked back and instantly said, of course. My dad asked this simple question back. He said, why? The student had no answer. In fact, my dad went around the room, and not a single student had a thoughtful answer to why he or she believed that the Bible is true. The session was done and my dad was walking toward the back of the auditorium, and this student comes running up to my father. He goes, Josh, Josh, I know the answer. I know why the Bible's true. My dad said, great, why is the Bible true?

paragraphs.heading: Because I think it is true
paragraphs.text: He looks at my father and he says, the Bible is true because I believe it. My dad said, wait a minute, the Bible's true because you believe it? What about a Quran and a Muslim who believes the Quran? This student looked my dad right back in the eyes and he said, if a Muslim believes the Quran is true, then the Quran is true for him. Now, my dad gave back to this student a memorable and powerful response. He said, here's the difference between me and you. You think the Bible is true because you believe it, but I believe the Bible because I think it is true.
You see, nothing is true or false because we believe it. Our beliefs don't change reality. But given how important truth is, let's hope that our beliefs match up with the reality.

paragraphs.heading: Close all windows
paragraphs.text: We've been talking about why truth is important, but let me share a story about my mom to help make this point really sink in. My mom has come a long way with technology, but she honestly used to be afraid of anything technologically speaking. In fact, when my mom got new technology, she would read the instructions letter by letter and follow them as best as she can. She got a computer, and up pops something that says, close all windows. My mom decides to, and I think you see where this is going, get up from her chair, walk around the house, and close all the windows in the house.

When she told the story, obviously a little bit embarrassed, we realize that truth has consequences. In this case it was embarrassment and confusion, but in many cases confusing truth can lead to devastating consequences. When we know truth, we're set free. We see a computer. It's created and designed to function a certain way. When we use it according to its design, then we're set free, we can accomplish things. But when we don't know its design, like in the story with my mom, what happens? Confusion, frustration, and sometimes significant consequences.

paragraphs.heading: What is real freedom?
paragraphs.text: I think one of the greatest lies and confusions of our age deals with the question of what is freedom. Have you ever thought in your life, what is real freedom? When I ask students to define freedom, typically they'll say to me, freedom is when you can do whatever you want to do as long as nobody is telling you how to live your life. If it feels good, do it, and you're free. Friends, that's not freedom. Living according to whatever feels good is going to enslave you to your passions. Real freedom is when we embrace God's design for our life, which is to love him and to love other people.

That's why Jesus said in John chapter three that if we live according to his design for our life, that we live in truth, our works will be made known to the world. Real freedom is not living according to whatever we think is right, but embracing God's design for our life. Real freedom is when we live in light of truth.

paragraphs.heading: Logic is careful reasoning
paragraphs.text: When you think of logic, who comes to mind? Probably somebody like Sherlock Holmes, who uses his wit and mind to outsmart his opponents. Maybe you feel this way when you've had a conversation with somebody with a different belief system, or when you're sharing your faith. It's as if it's this jockeying back and forth, trying to outsmart each other with logic. This can certainly happen, but technically logic is just a careful and proper use of reason. Logic is important for Christians so we can arrive at truthful beliefs ourselves, but it's also important in conversations with other people so we can help them arrive at truth in a loving manner. Let me share a story that might help.

paragraphs.heading: A conversation with a professor
paragraphs.text: Some time ago, when I was a graduate student studying philosophy, I had a memorable conversation with a professor from an Ivy League school. He said to me, oh, I think it's great that you're studying philosophy as a Christian. Maybe you'd want to study Buddhist philosophy, because all religions are true. Now, that struck me as very odd. I thought for a minute, wait a minute, how could all religions be true when they contradict on such fundamental teachings about God, the afterlife, and how you get salvation? So I simply asked him a question. I said, do you mind if I ask you a question? How could all religions be true, namely Islam and Christianity?

Muslims say if you believe Jesus is God, you've committed the sin of shirk, and you're certainly going to hell. I said, Christians say you can't get to heaven unless you believe Jesus is God. How can both of these be true? He kind of fumbled around a little bit. We kept talking. Eventually he looked at me and said, here's the deal. He said, religion aside, what really is true is cultural relativism. Therefore, you should be tolerant.

paragraphs.heading: Spotting the inconsistency
paragraphs.text: Now stop and think about this. Use your mind, your logic, to analyze this claim. He said he believed in cultural relativism, which says morality and truth depend upon the culture. But then he turned to me and said, therefore, because morality is relative, I should be tolerant. Now do you see the inconsistency? If morality is relative, he can't turn to me and say I ought to be tolerant, because he's appealing to tolerance as if it's a universal truth claim that everybody should follow. On the flip side, if he says that everybody should be tolerant, then he doesn't actually believe that morality is relative, because he's appealing to the universal principle or standard of tolerance.

Friends, people hold a lot of different views about God, religion, and morality, and one important thing to do is to listen to their views and draw them out. What we'll often see, when we do that, is that their views will lead to inconsistency and sometimes even to logical absurdity.

paragraphs.heading: Reducing a view to absurdity
paragraphs.text: For example, in Matthew 22:41 through 45, Jesus uses the known logical principle of reductio ad absurdum. Now, that sounds really fancy, but essentially what it means is reducing a position to absurdity. In this passage in Matthew, Jesus is having a conversation with the Pharisees, and he asks them, who do you think the Messiah is? Is the Messiah the son of David? And they say yes, the Messiah is the son of David. What Jesus says is meant to draw out their view to show that it leads to absurdity. Now, how does he do this?

He quotes from Psalms 110:1, in which David, who wrote that psalm, says that the Messiah is his Lord. And Jesus says, wait a minute, you just said that the Messiah is the son of David, but now we have David calling the Messiah Lord. How can that be? Now, what is Jesus' point? He's saying, if you think that the Messiah is merely the son of David, then that leads to absurdity. Rather, it's more reasonable to conclude that yes, the Messiah is the son of David, but he's more than human. He actually is Lord, as David himself said in Psalms 110 verse 1.

paragraphs.heading: Grow up in your thinking
paragraphs.text: In my conversation with an Ivy League professor, I was trying to show that he held two views in contradiction that, when drawn to their logical conclusion, led to absurdity. This is exactly what Jesus was doing with the Pharisees. This is why the Apostle Paul, in Ephesians 4 verses 14 through 15, says we are not to be like children in terms of our thinking, tossed to and fro by different waves of doctrine. Rather, we are to grow up and be mature in the way we think.

paragraphs.heading: Speak truth in love
paragraphs.text: Paul also says in this passage that we are to speak truth in love. In other words, we are called to speak truth. We can't compromise truth. We don't speak truth just to win arguments. We don't speak truth just to prove people wrong. We do it because we know that it's only truth that can set people free.

paragraphs.heading: A lifelong process
paragraphs.text: And please keep in mind, your conversations will not always go as smoothly as they seem to go with me and the Ivy League professor. In fact, more often than not, after a conversation I have with somebody, I'll step away and go, oh, I should have said this. Oh, next time, I'll say that. Learning to love God with our minds and use logic is a lifelong process. You're learning some powerful stuff about truth and defending the faith in this entire study that we're going through.

paragraphs.heading: Not to win arguments
paragraphs.text: It's easy to start thinking, great, I'm going to write this down, I'm going to go online, I'm going to go in person to my parents, my friends, other nonbelievers, and win some arguments. If that's what you're thinking, you're missing the point. The point of this is not to go out and win arguments. The point of this is, number one, to know truth for ourselves, and then second, to be able to speak that truth in love, to use reason, to use logic, to love people. That way, as people draw closer to you and learn more about your faith, they find something genuine and real that is not easily put out.

paragraphs.heading: Navigating a maze
paragraphs.text: Imagine you decide to try and navigate through a life-sized maze. Personally, I have no sense of direction and easily get lost, confused, and frustrated. In fact, I'd probably rather sit alone for an hour and just think and do nothing than try to make it through a maze alone. But if you had to go through a maze, what would make it easier to navigate? A guide would be helpful. It could help us know which steps to take as we try to get through the maze. A compass would be really nice. In fact, a compass would probably prevent us from getting lost, which is probably what would happen to me. Or a map would be super helpful, because a map would help us know exactly the path to be on from beginning to end. Essentially, what we would be looking for is someone or something to help us make it through the maze successfully.

paragraphs.heading: Your mental map
paragraphs.text: We constantly make choices every day based on our worldview: choices about how we treat people, how we spend our money, how we spend our time, whether we believe in God or not. These choices lead us on a certain path, and in the end we find ourselves at a specific destination. Now, there's no physical map for the maze of life, but we all have a mental map, a worldview, which is a set of beliefs that we have that helps us interpret and live in reality. So here's the critical question. How accurate is your mental map of reality, your worldview? Think about it. If you have a physical map and it doesn't match up, you're going to get lost and confused. But if your map does match up, you can make it through the maze successfully.

paragraphs.heading: Where did it come from?
paragraphs.text: We all carry around ideas which are part of our worldview and which shape our daily choices. Whether you're a Christian, an atheist, a Buddhist, or a Hindu, we all have a belief system that shapes the way that we live. You see, the question is not, do we have a worldview? The question is, what is our worldview, and where did it come from? From friends? From tradition? From family? From culture? Where does our worldview originate? With all these influences on our worldview, it's going to be critical to take a moment and examine our belief system more carefully.

paragraphs.heading: First, what is real?
paragraphs.text: There are a lot of different ways to examine the concept of a worldview, and our own worldviews in particular. Perhaps most helpful will be to consider four big questions that every worldview has to answer. First, what is real? What exists? Is reality only the physical world that we can touch, taste, see, and feel? Or is there a spiritual realm beyond the physical world? Is a human being just a body, or is there also a soul?

paragraphs.heading: Second, what is man?
paragraphs.text: Second, what is man? What does it mean to be human? Are we the product of blind evolutionary forces within nature? Or are we a part of the larger God consciousness and interconnected with all of reality? Or are we the personal creation of a loving God who made us in his image?

paragraphs.heading: Third, what happens at death?
paragraphs.text: Third, what happens at death? Where do we go, if anywhere, when we die? Maybe this is all there is, and death is final: when your heart stops beating, that's it. Or maybe you enter into some state of reincarnation until you finally reach nirvana. Or maybe when you die you face judgment before God and go to either heaven or hell for eternity. Every belief system has some claim about what happens when we die.

paragraphs.heading: Fourth, right and wrong
paragraphs.text: And fourth, what is the basis for right and wrong? Where does morality come from? Some believe that morality is relative, that there's no absolute standard outside of us, and that right and wrong comes from the individual or society. Others would point to karma, that we get rewarded or punished from actions we've done in the past and they carry on into the future. Whereas others believe that there's a standard outside of us, an objective standard that comes from either God's character or God's commands, which determines right from wrong.

paragraphs.heading: Isn't our worldview already set?
paragraphs.text: So why bother to think so deeply about our worldview? As Christians, isn't our worldview already set? Interestingly, and very importantly, studies show that people who describe themselves as Christians, in other words they check that box on a survey, live no differently from people who do not. But there's a segment of people who describe themselves as Christians that live differently. It's the Christians with a biblical worldview.

paragraphs.heading: See the world as Jesus saw it
paragraphs.text: That means if you want to live with the power of the gospel in your life, you need to see the world through the lens that Jesus saw it. If you see the world as Jesus did, in terms of our four big worldview questions and more, you'll be far more likely to live like Jesus. And if you live the way that Jesus wanted you to, you'll be far more likely to experience the freedom that he promised to those who follow him on the path of life.

paragraphs.heading: On top of a mountain
paragraphs.text: Think about the times where you felt most connected to God. Where was it? For many people, myself included, it's taken place on the top of a mountain. There's just something about being in nature, higher than normal, away from distractions, that we feel the presence of God. There's something powerful and spiritual about being on the top of a mountain.

paragraphs.heading: Mountaintops and founders
paragraphs.text: Interestingly, the great monotheistic religions all have traditions of a formative experience for their founder on a mountaintop. Take Judaism. Moses, arguably the most important prophet of the Old Testament, both saw God face to face and received the law on a mountaintop. In Islam, Muhammad, the founding prophet, claimed to receive the revelation from the angel Gabriel, which he wrote down as verses, or surahs, in the Quran. And Jesus gave some of his most important teaching on the Mount of Olives.

paragraphs.heading: What is real?
paragraphs.text: Like naturalism and pantheism, monotheism offers answers to our four big worldview questions. The first question is, what is real? Now, in naturalism, you'll remember that only physical things exist. On pantheism, all is divine. But on monotheism, there are both physical and non-physical things. There are material and immaterial entities. So rocks, dirt, trees, and other physical things are very real, but there's also a spiritual realm that includes God, angels, demons, and the soul.

paragraphs.heading: What is man?
paragraphs.text: The second worldview question is, what is man? Rather than seeing man as the result of this blind, purposeless evolutionary process, as naturalism claims, or a part of the oneness of the universe, as pantheism claims, monotheism states that we are the purposeful creation of a loving and personal God, and we uniquely reflect his character and image.

paragraphs.heading: What happens at death?
paragraphs.text: The third worldview question is, what happens at death? According to naturalism, humans simply face extinction. According to pantheism, we go through some kind of reincarnation until we enter the oneness of the universe. But on monotheism, when we die, we face judgment based upon God's standards and how we lived our lives, and then for eternity we either go to heaven or we go to hell.

paragraphs.heading: The basis for right and wrong
paragraphs.text: The fourth worldview question is, what is the basis for right and wrong? Unlike in pantheism and naturalism, on monotheism morality is not a human construct. Rather, morality comes from either the character or the commands of God. So there's a source outside of us that we are accountable to. We don't get to decide what is right and wrong, but we do get to decide if we're going to follow it.

paragraphs.heading: Has this God made himself known?
paragraphs.text: Essentially, monotheism says we are the purposeful creation of one God, and our lives now and for eternity depend upon how we respond to this God. Now, when we talk about monotheism, we're kind of talking about God in the abstract. The question is, has this one God made himself known? Has this God stepped into creation and revealed his plan and purpose for mankind?

paragraphs.heading: Star Wars and the force
paragraphs.text: Star Wars is one of the most successful film series in history. As a kid, I remember the epic battles between Luke Skywalker and Darth Vader. In fact, today I still enjoy bringing my own kids to the most recent Star Wars film. The cinematography, the special effects, and the storyline have captured generations. Star Wars also introduced the West to the worldview known as pantheism.

paragraphs.heading: All is divine
paragraphs.text: As we have seen, naturalism is the worldview that says only physical things exist and there are no supernatural forces. By contrast, pantheism is the worldview that says all is divine and there's no distinction between creator and creation. Like naturalism, pantheism offers answers to our four big worldview questions.

paragraphs.heading: What is real?
paragraphs.text: The first question is, what is real? On pantheism, all is divine. God is not a personal being whom we know, but is inseparable from the universe. God is more like a cosmic energy that pervades all things. Sound familiar? This is like the force in Star Wars.

paragraphs.heading: What is man?
paragraphs.text: In essence, all is one. Our second question is, what is man? If God is one with the universe and all is divine, then by necessity man is divine. Man is God. Pantheists will sometimes refer to human beings as gods or goddesses in embryo. So rather than seeing human beings as uniquely created in the image of God but broken by sin, pantheists see human beings as essentially good and divine.

paragraphs.heading: What happens at death?
paragraphs.text: Our third worldview question is, what happens at death? The goal of mankind on pantheism is to achieve enlightenment and to escape the cycle of reincarnation, and this is accomplished through practices such as channeling, meditation, and yoga. And then, like a drop falling into a river, we achieve enlightenment and become absorbed into the oneness of the universe.

paragraphs.heading: The basis for right and wrong
paragraphs.text: The fourth worldview question is, what is the basis for right and wrong? Since on pantheism all is one, distinctions are ultimately artificial. There is no distinction between creator and creation, between God and man, between right and wrong. Morality is an illusion. Since good and evil don't exist, ultimately morality is relative.

paragraphs.heading: Pantheism is nothing new
paragraphs.text: Like naturalism, pantheism is nothing new. Some of the ideas we see in the Star Wars films have their roots in ancient Eastern religions such as Hinduism and Buddhism. In fact, Paul likely addressed some pantheists in his speech at Mars Hill, as recorded in Acts chapter 17.
Pantheism is not new, but it is in direct conflict and contrast with the Christian worldview. The biggest question is, can it adequately capture reality as we know it and experience it?

paragraphs.heading: All that is or ever will be
paragraphs.text: A generation ago, in one of the most popular shows on TV, Cosmos, the host Carl Sagan began each episode by saying, the cosmos is all that is or was or ever will be. In a nutshell, Carl Sagan was describing the worldview known as naturalism, which is the view that all that exists is the physical material world, and in which there is no supernatural realm. Naturalism is clearly the predominant worldview in Western culture, shaping institutions like the educational system, the university, and even the media.

paragraphs.heading: What is real?
paragraphs.text: Naturalism offers non-supernatural answers to our four big worldview questions. First, what is real? According to naturalism, the only things that are real are those that can be tested by the five senses. In other words, only those things that have height, weight, extension in space, and other physical properties. So essentially, if something can't be weighed on a scale or seen through a microscope, it doesn't exist. So things like God, values, purposes, objective morality, demons, and the soul are not real. But of course things like grass, water, and sand are real.

paragraphs.heading: What is man?
paragraphs.text: So what is man? On naturalism, man is not the purposeful creation intended by a loving God, meant to be in relationship with God and with other people. In fact, the late atheist Victor Stenger captured the naturalistic view of man well. Darwinism implies that humanity developed by accident, contradicting the traditional teaching that humans are special, created in God's image. So essentially, that means that you and me and all of creation is a cosmic accident.

paragraphs.heading: What happens at death?
paragraphs.text: Now the third question is, what happens at death? There are really three options of what happens to you when you die. One would be to face some kind of judgment and go to either heaven or hell. The other possibility is to go through some kind of cycle of reincarnation. And the last possibility is extinction, that when you die you cease to exist. Now, on the naturalistic worldview, since there's no God and there's no soul, when you stop breathing your last breath, your life is done. Death is final.

paragraphs.heading: Dust in the wind
paragraphs.text: In the 1970s, the band Kansas had a famous song in which they described human beings as merely dust in the wind, and said that all our dreams are a mere curiosity. So we're like a drop of water in an endless sea. All that lasts forever is the earth below and the sky above.

paragraphs.heading: The basis for right and wrong
paragraphs.text: So then our fourth question is, what is the basis for right and wrong? Since naturalists don't believe in God, there's no standard outside of mankind that determines right and wrong. There are a variety of different attempts to explain morality from the naturalistic worldview, but essentially it boils down to what benefits mankind and helps propagate the species.

paragraphs.heading: Naturalism is nothing new
paragraphs.text: Naturalism is nothing new. In fact, centuries before the time of Christ there were some Greek philosophers who believed that all reality could be described as these small, tiny atoms. While naturalism may not be new, it is in direct contrast and conflict with a Christian worldview. The question is, can it capture reality, both as we experience it and know it to be?

paragraphs.heading: Is your faith threatened?
paragraphs.text: Have you ever felt like your faith is threatened when you walk into a science classroom? Maybe you've felt like science and faith are at odds, or you've even heard the narrative that science and faith are at war. Should we feel that way? It's easy to think that we ought to check our religious beliefs at the door when we come into the arena of science. But as tempting as this may be, this is not an option for a thoughtful Christian.

paragraphs.heading: Christianity and the birth of science
paragraphs.text: You might be pleasantly surprised to discover that it's actually the Christian worldview that is largely responsible for the birth of science. You see, there are certain ideas within the Judeo-Christian tradition that gave both the motivation and the intellectual backing for the birth of modern science. Many scientific pioneers, if not most, were motivated to do science because of their theistic, and in particular Christian, belief system. Scientific pioneers like Copernicus, Boyle, Galileo, Kepler, Newton, and many more did science because of their Christian worldview.

Francis Bacon believed God meant for us to explore the many mysteries that filled the natural world. Kepler wrote, "The chief aim of all investigations of the external world should be to discover the rational order which has been imposed on it by God, in which he revealed to us in the language of mathematics." Newton believed his scientific discoveries offered convincing evidence for the existence and creativity of God. "This most beautiful system of sun, planets, and comets could only proceed from the counsel and dominion of an intelligent and powerful being."

paragraphs.heading: Three reasons for the revolution
paragraphs.text: There are three main reasons why the scientific revolution took place in a culture shaped by a theistic worldview. The first is that Christianity in particular teaches that God is orderly, that he is rational in his very being, and that the universe is orderly. And since we're made in God's image, we are capable of understanding the world in which we live. The world is not chaotic, it's orderly.

Second, Christianity sanctioned science. In other words, science was done to care for and alleviate the suffering of human beings, and to protect and care for creation. And third, Christianity gave the motivation that science was to be done to bring glory to God. Despite the common narrative that we hear, that science is at odds with faith, it's actually the Christian worldview that contributed enormously to the rise of science.

paragraphs.heading: Naturalism undermines science
paragraphs.text: Naturalism actually undermines science. Charles Darwin once said, "But then with me the horrid doubt always arises whether the convictions of man's mind, which has been developed from the mind of lower animals, are of any value or at all trustworthy. Would anyone trust in the convictions of a monkey's mind, if there are any convictions in such a mind?" In other words, what Darwin is saying is that his very naturalistic evolutionary theory undermines any basis we have for concluding that evolution is true.

Now here's why. According to this naturalistic theory, the brain is the result of this blind, purposeless material process. It's a large accident. So this raises a troubling question: how do you know we can trust anything that the brain tells us is true? This isn't a problem for the Christian worldview, because God is reasonable, the world is orderly, and we've been made in God's image to understand the world in which we're placed. Naturalists can do science, but they have to borrow from the Judeo-Christian worldview to do so.

paragraphs.heading: Where science and theology overlap
paragraphs.text: Science and faith are not at odds. There certainly are distinct scientific and distinct theological questions. For example, in science, the question of how many oxygen atoms are in a water molecule, or in theology, what is the nature of an angel? Those are distinct questions that belong in their own discipline. But there are times when science and theology overlap, questions such as the origin of the universe, the origin of mankind, and the historical resurrection. Sometimes science and faith intersect.

paragraphs.heading: God's two books
paragraphs.text: The idea that Christianity is at war with science is mistaken. It's a misreading of the historical, scientific, theological, and philosophical evidence. Christians have always taught that God speaks through two books, the book of nature and the book of Scripture. The book of nature means that God has made himself known in creation. Creation speaks truths about the Creator, but God has also made himself known through the Scriptures. God's word reveals truth about his character and also his design for mankind. We can certainly misinterpret the Scriptures and we can misunderstand the scientific evidence. But when done accurately, both books reveal truths about the Creator.

paragraphs.heading: The cabin in the woods
paragraphs.text: Imagine you go for a hike and come across a cabin. It looks interesting, so you decide to explore. But as you grow closer, you notice something strange: you hear your favorite song playing inside. When you open the door, you see shoes and a jacket fitted perfectly for you. On the table are the books and magazines you like to read. In the refrigerator are your favorite snacks, and in the bathroom you find all the toiletries you normally use. Everything you need to survive, tailored just to your liking, is there.

How did the cabin get arranged so precisely? Maybe you just got lucky and all of this is coincidence. But that doesn't seem very reasonable if you think about it for a minute, does it? There are just too many things tailored precisely for you. You might not know why or who did it, but clearly there's some purpose and design behind the arrangement of this cabin.

paragraphs.heading: A universe on a razor's edge
paragraphs.text: Freeman J. Dyson, a renowned theoretical physicist, once said, "As we look out into the universe and identify the many accidents of physics and astronomy that have worked to our benefit, it almost seems as if the universe must in some sense have known that we were coming." The laws of physics and astronomy all exist within a very small range to allow the universe to support life. It's as if these laws exist on a razor's edge: the slightest change to the left or the right and the entire universe becomes inhospitable to life.

paragraphs.heading: The water balloon launcher
paragraphs.text: When I was in college, some friends of mine lived on the third story of an apartment building, with a window overlooking a parking lot, a tall row of trees, a big water gutter, and then a stop sign. They thought it'd be entertaining to open their window, use one of those huge water balloon launchers, and launch balloons at cars as they came home. One evening we launched one from the window. It cleared the water gutter, the trees, and the parking lot, and hit a car right on the windshield and cracked it. And yes, we had to pay for it.

Imagine how many factors we had to get right to hit our target. What if there was more water in the balloon? We wouldn't have gone far enough. If there was less water, we would have gone too far. What if we were up in the mountains, where the air pressure is different? That would have gone further. What if the tension in the launcher was different? There are all these things we had to get right to hit our target.

That's not too different from our universe as a whole. The universe has been expanding at a very carefully calibrated rate since its inception, but if that rate were different in comparison with the mass density or with the dark energy, we couldn't even have a universe capable of supporting life. So what are the mathematical odds that a universe with its laws of physics and cosmology randomly generated would be capable of having stars, which are necessary for there to be life? According to astrophysicist Lee Smolin, the odds are 1 times 10 to the 229th power.

Do you realize how big that number is? That's one with 229 zeros after it. Essentially, it's equivalent to taking every single proton in the entire universe, each proton representing its own universe with randomly generated laws of physics. Mathematically speaking, none of those universes would be capable of generating stars, which means they wouldn't be capable of having life.

paragraphs.heading: Finding a coin blindfolded
paragraphs.text: But let's compare this to our cabin. What if you were blindfolded in this cabin, trying to find a lost coin? What are the odds that you could find it? Now expand the search to the city I'm in, or the country, or the entire planet, our solar system, our galaxy, the entire universe. What are the mathematical odds that, blindfolded, you could find this coin? You realize it is far more likely that you would find this coin than that we would find ourselves in a universe with randomly generated laws capable of supporting complex life.

paragraphs.heading: Chance or law?
paragraphs.text: There's very little debate that our universe is exquisitely fine-tuned. The question is what best explains the fine-tuning. One option people often give is chance, but we've seen clearly, mathematically, that this is not a reasonable explanation. Another option is law: maybe there's some law that requires the other laws to be fine-tuned for life. But the problem is that laws in physics and cosmology tend to create things that are simple and repeatable, not complex and specified like the laws that govern our universe.

paragraphs.heading: The multiverse
paragraphs.text: One final option often used to explain away fine-tuning is the multiverse, the idea that there are either a ton of universes out there or an infinite number of them, so we shouldn't be surprised that we happen to find ourselves in a universe fine-tuned for life. There are a couple of problems with appealing to this. One is that there's no direct scientific evidence for the multiverse; at this stage it's scientific conjecture. But even if we do find evidence for it, that wouldn't explain away design. All it would do is move design away from this universe to the multiverse. There would still need to be an explanation for why there is a multiverse that generates individually fine-tuned universes.

paragraphs.heading: A fine tuner
paragraphs.text: If we're trying to explain away the design of a car and somebody says, "Oh, we can explain it away by a factory," you'd say, wait a minute, there still needs to be a sufficient explanation for the factory. Rather than law, chance, or the multiverse explaining away fine-tuning, I think the best explanation is that there is a fine tuner who organized the universe with us in mind. Just as the arrangement of the cabin pointed toward somebody expecting our arrival, the exquisite fine-tuning of life best points toward someone expecting us to live here, and even to feel at home.

paragraphs.heading: The most complex system in the room
paragraphs.text: Take a look at the room around you and ask yourself a simple question. What do you think is the most complex system that stores the most information? Maybe there's a computer in the room, maybe there's a tablet, maybe you're streaming this on your cell phone. Are those the most complex systems that store vast amounts of information? The answer is clearly no. The most complex system in the room is you. To be specific, it's your DNA.

DNA stores information, much of the information that makes you, you. In fact, DNA has greater storage capacity than any technology humans have ever created. Take, for example, just one gram of DNA. It has roughly the storage capacity of half a million movies. Now that blows your smartphone away.

paragraphs.heading: Nine feet in a single cell
paragraphs.text: Your body is made up of around 100 trillion cells. The DNA in one cell of your body, just one cell, if it were unwound, would be about nine feet in length. That means all the DNA in your body strung together would go from here to the sun and back about 70 times. This raises a very troubling and difficult question, both for naturalism and for pantheism: what can best explain the source of this vast amount of information? What worldview best explains the origin of DNA?

paragraphs.heading: Monkeys typing Shakespeare
paragraphs.text: To explain the rise of information that we see in nature, some naturalists have devised a test simply called the monkeys typing Shakespeare theorem. The idea is that if you have a bunch of monkeys and enough computers and enough time, eventually one of the monkeys will sit down, through a purely blind lucky process, and type out all the works of Shakespeare. The point is to explain the rise of information in nature, and in DNA specifically, through a purely blind process.

paragraphs.heading: What chance can actually produce
paragraphs.text: In my book Understanding Intelligent Design, my co-author William Dembski and I cited a quantum computational physicist by the name of Seth Lloyd. What Seth Lloyd did is mathematically compute exactly how much information could arise by chance, given all the resources of the universe. He concluded that chance alone could not produce all the works of Shakespeare. It couldn't produce one work of Shakespeare, not a chapter, not a page, not a paragraph. All the resources of the universe by chance at best could produce four lines from one work of Shakespeare: "To be or not to be, that is the question. Whether 'tis nobler in the mind to suffer."

paragraphs.heading: Someone actually ran the experiment
paragraphs.text: Some time ago some students and a professor decided to actually test the monkeys typing Shakespeare theorem. They took some monkeys and put them in a zoo with some old computers and typewriters to see if one of the monkeys would sit down and type out Romeo and Juliet or Hamlet. The first monkey picked up a rock, climbed up on the computer and tried to bash it. Some other monkeys climbed up on top and actually went to the bathroom on the computer. But before you discount this experiment: in the time that they were in there, these monkeys produced roughly six pages of written text: a string of A's, L's, M's, J's and an occasional S. Not a single word.

paragraphs.heading: A message in the sand
paragraphs.text: In reality, whenever we come across information and can trace it back to its causal source, we always find a mind. Imagine you come visit me in Southern California and we go walking on the beach. All of a sudden we stop, because we see engraved in the sand a heart that says "Sean loves Stephanie." Stephanie is my wife. Now, I know none of you would stop and say, "That's crazy. I've heard about earthquakes in Southern California, but I had no idea that when the ground shook, messages arose from the deep." None of you would try to explain that message by the tides or the water or the wind. You would know that the only plausible explanation for those markings is an intelligent mind.

We know this in our daily lives: whenever we see information at its source, we find a mind. You get a text and it's legible, and you trace it back to a texter. Look at the information in a book and you trace it back to an author. Read a blog and you trace it back to a blogger. If you go outside and the clouds say "drink Coke," none of you think, oh my goodness, a storm is coming from the east. Rather, you know that that information was put there by an intelligent mind, in this case by a pilot.

paragraphs.heading: An author of life
paragraphs.text: We find more information in DNA than in anything humans can invent. That's why the best explanation for the DNA we see in nature, and in the human body in particular, is that it comes from an intelligent designer, an author of life.

paragraphs.heading: A canyon and a city
paragraphs.text: Imagine you go hiking in a desert canyon. You see some rocks, some cacti, maybe some caves in the canyon sides. What would you conclude is the best explanation for the features you saw before you? Obviously you'd think that natural forces, wind, erosion, maybe water, were at work. But what if you went hiking into a desert canyon and this time carved into the walls was an ancient city? Now what would you conclude? There actually is a place like this.

It's the ancient city of Petra, which is found in the country of Jordan. When modern day explorers came across Petra, do you think they stopped and thought, oh my goodness, this is the result of natural forces? Of course not. When you look at Petra today, you can see intricately carved pillars and buildings in the side of the solid rock. You can see tombs and even a complex tunnel system for water.

paragraphs.heading: Specified complexity
paragraphs.text: So why do we recognize design in the city of Petra but not in a typical canyon? Petra has a feature that we call specified complexity. It might sound daunting, but it's actually common sense and intuitive. If something is specified, it has a particular pattern. For example, crystals are specified according to a certain pattern. Shells are specified according to a pattern. Even pulsars emit light at regular intervals. But nobody looks at these and assumes design, because they lack complexity. They can easily be explained by the regular workings of the laws of nature.

When something is complex, it has multiple parts. Take, for example, a pile of rocks. Any pile of rocks is actually quite complex, but we don't assume that a pile of rocks is designed, because it lacks specified complexity.

Design requires both specificity and complexity. Natural forces alone can result in things being specified with a pattern, such as the crystals we've seen, and natural forces can bring about things that are complex, like a pile of rocks. But natural forces cannot create things with specified complexity, such as Petra. When we see something as intricate as the ancient city of Petra, we know that the best explanation is that it is the result of an intelligent designer.

paragraphs.heading: Forensics and archaeology
paragraphs.text: This is how many scientific fields operate. Take forensic science, for example. When a forensic scientist comes across a body, he or she asks two questions. Is it the result of natural causes, such as a heart attack? Or is it the result of intelligent activity, homicide? The forensic scientist will look for signs of specified complexity to come to the most reasonable explanation. Archaeologists do the same thing. When an archaeologist comes across some kind of ancient relic, he or she asks, is this the result of natural forces, or is it the result of design? They will look at the physical features of, say, a rock that they find, and if they find specified complexity such as you would see on an arrowhead, then the archaeologist will conclude that the best explanation is that this is the result of intelligent design.

paragraphs.heading: The same pattern in nature
paragraphs.text: Amazingly, we find the same patterns of design in nature itself. Just take the human body. In every single cell we find DNA, and in DNA, as we have seen, we have both specificity and complexity. In fact, there is more information in DNA than in anything humans are close to creating. The best explanation for DNA is that it was designed by a creator of life. There are many other examples of design, such as we see in the Cambrian explosion, in irreducibly complex systems, and even in the origin of the universe itself.

paragraphs.heading: The God of the gaps objection
paragraphs.text: This is why one of the most common objections against intelligent design fails. You may have heard people say, well, you're just making an argument from the gaps. It's called the God of the gaps, and the idea is that we look at nature, we don't have a natural explanation, and so we assume God. But that's not what we're doing. We're not looking at nature and saying, well, we lack an explanation for DNA, or we lack an explanation for fine-tuning, therefore God did it.

We're essentially saying two things. Number one, nature can't explain it alone. But we also see the positive evidence of an intelligent agent. We look at DNA, we see specified complexity. We look at the fine-tuning of the laws of physics, we see specified complexity. And as we have seen, when we see that marker, we know the best explanation is that it is the result of an intelligent designer.

paragraphs.heading: Where naturalism and pantheism fail
paragraphs.text: Both naturalism and pantheism fail to adequately explain design in nature for one basic reason: they lack an intelligent agent, a cosmic mind that can produce specified complexity. In fact, they have to rely entirely upon chance, time and the laws of nature. But this is like trying to rely upon wind, erosion, water and other natural forces to explain the ancient city of Petra. The most reasonable explanation for design in nature is that the world was actually designed.

paragraphs.heading: The heavens declare
paragraphs.text: Design in nature points toward a designer. This, of course, should come as no surprise to those of us who believe in God. After all, long before the discoveries of modern science, the psalmist wrote that the heavens declare the glory of God, the skies proclaim his majesty, day by day they spew forth speech, night by night they display knowledge. In other words, the psalmist knew that the natural world reveals truths about the Creator.
If the world really is designed, if the natural world is actually filled with specified complexity, then this raises a very important question. Who is this designer?

paragraphs.heading: Can you be good without God?
paragraphs.text: Can you be good without God? Do you need to believe in God to know morality? Does the existence of a moral law point toward a moral law giver? Or can morality be explained by evolution? These are some of the most common and yet important questions we can ask.

In Romans chapter 2, the Apostle Paul says that even people without the law know right and wrong, because it's written on their hearts. In other words, part of being human is that we know there's a moral law. In fact, we know it so clearly, says Paul, that God can judge us based upon it. So in Romans 1, Paul says that creation points toward a creator, and now in Romans 2 he says that the existence of a moral law that we know clearly points toward a moral law giver.

paragraphs.heading: What the argument is not
paragraphs.text: Let's take a minute and flesh this out. When developed, this is referred to as the moral argument for the existence of God. Keep something in mind before we look at the particulars. We're not saying that people have to believe in God to be moral. We're not saying that people have to believe in God to know right from wrong. Atheists can be moral. Pantheists can be moral. Christians can be immoral. But we are arguing that if there is an objective moral standard, then there must be a God.

Think about it. You can read a book if you don't believe in authors; all you need to do is know how to read. But the question is, can there be such things as books if there are no authors? The answer to that is obviously no. Similarly, people can be moral if they don't believe in God. That's not the interesting question. The question is, can there be a real right and wrong, an objective morality, if there is no God? The answer to that is no.

paragraphs.heading: If there is no God
paragraphs.text: In his classic novel The Brothers Karamazov, Russian novelist Fyodor Dostoevsky famously said, if there is no God, all is permissible. In other words, if there's not a transcendent moral source outside of human beings, then anything goes. The late atheist philosopher Friedrich Nietzsche said that if there is no God, then it's those with power who get to determine right and wrong. In other words, if God doesn't exist, then it's those with the biggest guns who get to determine morality.

paragraphs.heading: The first premise
paragraphs.text: So here's the moral argument for the existence of God stated more formally. It has two premises and a conclusion. The first premise is that if there are objective moral values and duties, then God must exist. So what is it about morality that points toward God? For one, moral values and duties aren't physical. You can't weigh them, they don't have extension in space, they can't be studied by science. Moral values and duties contain information, commands about how we are supposed to live. They point toward a source outside of mankind, instructing us about how we're supposed to behave. There's something about moral values and duties that has a spiritual core.

paragraphs.heading: The second premise
paragraphs.text: The second premise is that objective moral values and duties exist. How can I make such a claim? There are two reasons. For one, in his classic book The Abolition of Man, C.S. Lewis famously pointed out that across cultures throughout the history of the world there's a commitment to certain universal moral principles: that justice is better than injustice, that courage is good, that we ought to care for our children and our posterity. As Lewis points out, how we practice those moral principles might vary across culture, but there is a universal agreement and commitment to the underlying moral principles.

Second, people simply know that there's a right and wrong. We all live as if we believe morality is objective. My dad often has said to me, son, you know what people believe about right and wrong not by what they say, not by what they do, but by how they want to be treated. Everybody wants to be treated as if promise keeping is an objective feature of the universe. So I often tell my students, if someone says to you there's no such thing as objective morality, cut in front of them in line. What are they going to say? That's not fair. That's not right, as if there's a moral standard that we're all supposed to follow.

paragraphs.heading: A debate about morality
paragraphs.text: A few years ago I sponsored a public debate with three of my high school students and three students from the public school free-thinking atheist agnostic club. They debated the historical Jesus, intelligent design, and morality. One of my students got up there and said, there is an objective moral law, we know it, therefore there's a moral law giver. Morality points toward God. Then one of their students got up there and said, there is no objective moral law. In fact, morality is all subjective. It's like picking an ice cream flavor. You have your moral truth and I have mine, and we all live accordingly.

And then he sat down. When it was time for the concluding speech, instead of summarizing why he thought their team won, one of the free thinking students got up there and this is what he said: you Christians are bigoted, hateful and intolerant, shame on you for the way that you live. I sat there and I thought, wait a minute. Just moments before, he said morality is subjective, it's entirely individualistic and there's no objective standard. Then he got up there and said, you Christians have violated every single moral norm, shame on you, you should have known differently. His worldview said there's no such thing as objective moral values and duties, but he couldn't live it out consistently.

paragraphs.heading: What the argument shows
paragraphs.text: Simply put, this argument shows that the best explanation for the existence of objective moral values and duties is that there is a personal God. Now, this alone doesn't prove that the Christian God exists. It raises challenges for both pantheism and naturalism, but broadly speaking it's consistent with a God of Judaism and a God of Islam. What this argument shows is that the physical world is not all that exists. There is a spiritual and a moral realm. There is a God who cares about the way that we live. There is a God who will hold us accountable for how we live our lives.

paragraphs.heading: The most beautiful thing
paragraphs.text: Think of the most beautiful thing you can imagine. Is it a rose, a snow-capped mountain, a rhythmic dance or a distant galaxy? For me, I think of Glacier Bay in Alaska. It's magnificent and it's truly beautiful. I also think of the aqua colored water and the coral in the Caribbean. Regardless of what came to your mind, I doubt any of you, when I asked the question, thought, beauty? I don't believe there are real beautiful things in the world. The reality is we all actually believe in objective beauty.

paragraphs.heading: In the eye of the beholder?
paragraphs.text: And yet, interestingly, when asked, most people would say they agree with the statement that beauty is in the eye of the beholder. So which is it? Is beauty a real part of the world in which we live, or is it entirely a matter of personal preference, like choosing an ice cream flavor? If you find yourself agreeing with the statement that beauty is in the eye of the beholder, then you need to at least realize that you are in the minority in terms of history. That's right. Most thinkers from a variety of traditions have believed that there are three transcendentals that stand outside of human opinion: goodness, truth, and beauty. And if beauty really exists, then there's good reason to believe there's a God, or some kind of divine artist, responsible for making the world beautiful.

paragraphs.heading: But people disagree
paragraphs.text: You might be thinking, wait a minute, how can beauty be objective, a real feature of the world, when people differ over what they think is beautiful? After all, when it comes to music taste, some people like rap and other people like country. When it comes to art, some people like paintings of landscapes where other people like art that is more abstract. How can beauty be real when there's such disagreement?

At first this seems like a strong objection, but keep a couple of things in mind. First, nothing follows logically from disagreement. People disagree over all sorts of things, but does that mean there's no truth? Take science and history. People differ over what is historically true and over what is scientific fact. Does that mean there are no facts and there's no truth? Of course not. We could spend all day arguing over which of these two flowers is most beautiful. What would come of it? Probably not much. But we would still agree that there's such a thing as beauty. We would still agree that flowers can possess that property, and in fact we would agree that flowers many times really are beautiful.

paragraphs.heading: Agreement beneath the disagreement
paragraphs.text: Second, what do we do with disagreements? Music tastes, for example. There is still general agreement that certain rhythmic patterns, structures and arrangements are necessary for music to be beautiful. And while people may disagree over what particular features of a person are beautiful, there is agreement that human beings can truly be beautiful. The universal recognition of beauty in nature, crashing waves, a sunset or a rose, must not be missed.

paragraphs.heading: We speak as if beauty is real
paragraphs.text: Even though we may disagree on the particulars, we certainly speak as if we think beauty is objective. When we say a rose is beautiful, we speak as if we think there's some property or characteristic that the rose itself possesses. When we talk about a poem being beautiful, we seem to be indicating that we think there's a quality of the poem itself that is beautiful. In other words, when we say that something is beautiful, we mean that that individual thing has the universal property of beauty. So when I say to my wife, you are beautiful, I mean that she has a property of beauty, something she possesses as a person, and her beauty is just as real a feature of her as the fact that she has a certain height and a certain eye color. You might not quite be fully convinced yet, but you do have to admit that we at least speak as if we believe that beauty is real.

paragraphs.heading: Can naturalism explain beauty?
paragraphs.text: So here's the question: can pantheism and naturalism adequately explain beauty? According to naturalism, our ability to recognize beauty is some evolved trait that we inherited from our ancestors. At first glance this might seem reasonable. After all, if a species of beings found their environment pleasing, they would be more likely to survive, arguably. The problem is we don't just find the world pleasing, we find it beautiful. We explore the depths of the ocean and we peer into the most distant galaxies and we regularly find beauty. The world is filled with beauty, but it's seemingly gratuitous beauty that has no survival value.

What about pantheism? Can it adequately explain beauty? As you will remember, on pantheism all is one, so there's really no distinctions in nature that are real. What that means is there's no genuine difference between beauty and ugliness. So rather than accounting for why we find beauty in nature, pantheism simply explains beauty away as an illusion.

paragraphs.heading: A divine artist
paragraphs.text: The Christian worldview takes beauty seriously. Since God himself is beautiful and he has crafted the world with purpose and order, we should expect to find beauty in creation. And that is exactly what we find: the splendor of a waterfall, the magnificence of a diamond or the grandeur of a sequoia tree. The world is filled with beauty. Just take a look at the world around you, or even take out your smartphone and look at the photos. Our hearts resonate when we experience beauty. The existence of real beauty in the world may not prove that God exists, but it is one powerful pointer that the world has been fashioned with purpose, order, and beauty by a divine artist.

paragraphs.heading: Beliefs that keep popping up
paragraphs.text: "All right, thanks. Sounds good." There are certain beliefs that we as human beings hold to deeply. We believe in the value of truth. We believe that beauty and morality are objective. And we believe that we are agents that make genuine, free decisions that are up to us. The problem is that some of us embrace certain worldviews that lead to a denial of those common sense beliefs in practice. But when we deny those common sense beliefs, they keep popping up to the surface.

So think of it like a beach ball. If you take a beach ball and you try to push it under the water, what happens? It keeps popping up to the surface. You can't hold it down forever. The same thing happens with people who embrace worldviews that lead to the denial of common sense. These beliefs are going to pop up.

paragraphs.heading: Why naturalism can't account for agency
paragraphs.text: Why can't naturalism account for agency? Think about it. On naturalism there is no immaterial soul. There's no self distinct from nature that can make meaningful, genuinely free choices. Although humans are more complex, ultimately they are a purely physical object, like water. When water is poured into a glass, what happens? Does it consider its options? Does it decide its shape or temperature? Of course not. Because of the laws of nature and the molecular structure of water, it will fit to the shape of the glass. In naturalism, we human beings are like this water: purely physical objects whose behavior and beliefs and actions simply conform to the physical structure around us. There is no agency. There are no genuine choices that we make as persons.

paragraphs.heading: Sam Harris writes a book
paragraphs.text: In fact, this is why many atheists will recognize and admit that if atheism is true, agency is out the window. Sam Harris, one of the most well-known atheists today, in his book titled Free Will, says, quote, free will is an illusion. I have to wonder, why did Harris even bother to write the book? After all, when you write a book, you think that you're writing down ideas that are genuinely up to you, and the goal is to persuade other people, other agents, to adopt your viewpoints. The very point of writing a book assumes that people can be persuaded freely by your ideas. And yet the premise of his entire book is that we don't have free will, that we're not genuinely free agents. So again, his worldview says we are not agents, but his actions portray and reveal his true beliefs.

paragraphs.heading: Pantheism obliterates choice
paragraphs.text: At this stage, the problems with pantheism should be familiar. Since pantheism teaches that all is one, there is no self distinct from nature that can act purposefully. So at its core, pantheism obliterates the idea of a free being that can make real choices.

"I would love the spaghetti with meatballs." "Comes with soup or salad?" "Salad, please." "You can do house dressing, you can do Caesar, you can do ranch." "Let's go with house dressing on the side. Thank you."

paragraphs.heading: Do you really make choices?
paragraphs.text: Let me ask you a question. Do you really believe that you are an agent who makes genuinely free choices that are up to you? Do you think you make choices, whether they're big or they're small, that really come from your own agency? Of course you do. In the big and in the small choices of life, we all know that our decisions matter, and that many of those decisions, in fact all of those decisions, are up to us.

Imagine you're a high school senior rushing down the hall by the lockers, trying to get to class on time, and seemingly out of nowhere a freshman bumps into you, knocks you over, and your books go all over the floor. Would it make a difference if you found out that that freshman tripped, as opposed to intentionally knocking you over? Imagine after class your teacher takes you aside and very sincerely says, I want to compliment you on doing a great job in class today. Your homework, the way you did on your test, your score, and even your discussion was fantastic, good for you. It would make a difference if you found out that this teacher was assigned by the state to give one compliment a day and your name happened to come up alphabetically. What if someone you really liked asked you out to prom, but you found out later that this person was forced to ask you by his parents? Would that make a difference?

Look, the answer to all these questions is obviously yes. We know that our ability to make choices and act as agents matters. In fact, if we can't make choices that are up to us, virtues that we care about so deeply, like love and mercy and courage and sacrifice, lose their meaning. If we lose agency, everything of value is gone.

paragraphs.heading: Monotheism accounts for agency
paragraphs.text: Of all the worldviews, monotheism best accounts for agency. The world is, after all, the free creation of a personal agent, God, and we have been made in his image and given the responsibility and ability to make choices. We are not simply part of nature. We are agents who make meaningful choices within nature.

paragraphs.heading: Great power, great responsibility
paragraphs.text: My favorite superhero by far is Spider-Man, also known as Peter Parker. His uncle, Ben Parker, once said to him, with great power comes great responsibility. As human beings we have been given great power. We have the ability to make meaningful choices that deeply affect the world that we live in, and with that great power does come great responsibility. We have responsibility to one another as human beings, and if there is a divine agent, God, we just might have responsibility to him too.

paragraphs.heading: A story I made up
paragraphs.text: I will never forget February 14th, Valentine's Day of my sophomore year in high school. It began like any other day, but little did I realize that a choice I would make that day would shape the course of my life forever. No, I have to be honest, I completely made that up. I don't remember anything from Valentine's Day my sophomore year in high school. But chances are you listened up. Why? Because you thought I was going to tell a story.

paragraphs.heading: Why we love stories
paragraphs.text: Isn't it interesting how much we love stories, whether it's an enthralling novel, a captivating movie or a story from a friend? We listen to stories, we love stories and we tell stories. There's something about a story that's irresistible. We hear a story and it draws us in and demands our attention. In fact, that's probably one reason why Jesus was so influential. He told powerful, memorable stories that we can relate to: the story of the prodigal son, the story of the Good Samaritan. Any good speaker will tell you that if they want to have an impact on the audience, they've got to tell powerful stories.

paragraphs.heading: Storytelling creatures
paragraphs.text: Stories are so central to human existence that it's accurate to say we are storytelling creatures. Think about it. Movies are stories. Songs tell stories. Commercials are stories. Politicians compete to tell the best stories about who will serve in office. Lawyers will try to tell the best story about the person on trial. Businessmen sell products by telling stories. Even kids, when they play make-believe, they play make-believe in stories. Our lives are stories. But stories are not based on a series of random, disconnected, meaningless events. Stories are about conflict and resolution.
