paragraphs.text: In 1873, a priest by the name of Father Damien heard about a colony of lepers who were living and dying without anybody to care for them. So, with full awareness of the risk, Father Damien went and became a priest for this colony of lepers. He prayed for them. He preached to them. He changed their wounds. He built caskets. He buried many of them. For 12 years, with deep compassion and care, he loved this colony of lepers, so they would know and experience the love of God. One Sunday evening, however, everything changed. Father Damien stood before the people with leprosy and he spoke these two words. He said, "We lepers." He opened up his robe and showed the first physical signs of leprosy. Father Damien had become a leper.

Let me ask you a couple of questions about the story. First, how did the view of the lepers change toward Father Damien when he became a leper? No doubt, beforehand they knew that he loved them. They saw his willingness to sacrifice everything for them, but now, when he got leprosy, everything was different. Now he could understand them in a new way. They saw the depth of his sacrifice for them. He could empathize with them in a personal way.

paragraphs.heading: God is right there with us
paragraphs.text: The second question is, is God's response to our suffering more like Father Damien before he got leprosy, or after? If we stop and we think about the life, ministry and death of Jesus, I think the answer is clear. It's after. See, God didn't just send a prophet or an angel or a book, as important as those are. In the person of Jesus Christ, God came down personally and has experienced our pain. We are not abandoned to our suffering and our pain. So part of the answer to "where is God when I suffer" is that God is right there suffering with us.

paragraphs.heading: A God who has suffered
paragraphs.text: Think about the symbols for the various world religions. You've got the statue of Buddha for Buddhism, the gate for Shintoism, the crescent and the sword for Islam, or the Star of David for Judaism. Yet for Christianity, the most defining image, the most defining symbol, is the cross: a picture of the creator of the universe stepped down in human flesh, suffering for us. We follow and worship a God who has suffered.

Isaiah the prophet said the coming Messiah would be a man of sorrows, familiar with suffering. And in the book of Hebrews, the author writes in chapter 4 that we do not follow a high priest who's unable to sympathize with us, but we have a high priest who's been tempted and tested in every way like we are. He understands our weaknesses, but is without sin.

If you're ever tempted to think that God doesn't understand your suffering or your pain, you might think again. For example, if you're in physical pain and you think, gosh, I'm in so much pain, God doesn't understand what I'm going through, remember that Jesus was crucified and experienced excruciating physical pain. If you've gone through relational difficulties, and maybe somebody's betrayed you or left you out, and you think, God, you don't understand, remember that during his lifetime much of Jesus' family didn't believe in him, and in fact he was betrayed by one of his closest disciples. Jesus understands.

Many times what our suffering enables us to do is to have empathy for other people and build a deeper sense of community. Take the example of Father Damien contracting leprosy. As painful and as hurtful as that is, it enabled him to be in a new community and experience the love of a people that wasn't there before.

paragraphs.heading: Will you trust me?
paragraphs.text: Ultimately, I might not be able to explain why you, or me, or anyone else experiences a particular kind of suffering. Sometimes we might know in this life, but many times it won't be until we get to eternity. But I know this. I know that God is good. I know that God has not abandoned us in our suffering. I know God is asking you and me the same question he asked Job thousands of years ago, when Job was suffering immensely. He said, Job, will you trust me?

paragraphs.heading: What you meant for evil
paragraphs.text: It's important to remember that God can take our greatest pain, our greatest suffering, and turn it to good. We see this in the life of Joseph, a story that you know. Joseph is sold into slavery by his own brothers and ends up in prison, but rises up through God's hand to be second in command in Egypt, and is able to save his family from famine. When he finally talks with his brothers and they realize his identity, they're afraid that he might take retribution against them. But what does he say? He essentially says, don't worry. What you meant for evil, God meant for good.

When Jesus was arrested and crucified, his apostles thought that all had been lost. This movement and person they had been following for roughly three years seemingly had come to an end. They were devastated. But what they didn't realize at that moment is that in their darkest hour, God had never let go of the steering wheel. He was still in control and working his greatest good. We see it's through the resurrection that we know that death does not have the end. Suffering is not the end, and this world will ultimately be redeemed.

paragraphs.heading: Death, where is your sting?
paragraphs.text: Suffering and pain do not have the final word. Jesus is risen. That's right, Jesus is risen. That's why the Apostle Paul, who experienced tremendous suffering, could shout with an air of defiance in 1 Corinthians 15, a chapter on the resurrection: "Death, where's your victory? Death, where's your sting?"

paragraphs.heading: A good person in hell
paragraphs.text: Not long ago I was speaking at a student conference, and afterwards a young man came up to me who was deeply troubled about the idea of hell. He just couldn't reconcile that a loving God would send a good person to hell. I did my best to answer his questions. We talked probably 30 or 40 minutes, and it dawned on me: his problem was that he viewed people as being essentially good. He kind of looked at God as if God is looking down, and if someone does the slightest small thing, that person goes to hell for eternity. He viewed it as if there are a few really bad people, like Hitler, out there, but the rest of us are essentially good, and so hell seemed like total overkill. Although it might surprise you, I actually agree with him, in the sense that it would be total overkill for God to send a good person to hell.

paragraphs.heading: No one is good
paragraphs.text: But the problem is that the Bible has a very different view of human nature. In Romans chapter 3, Paul says that no one is righteous, no one is good, all have turned away from God. And in Mark chapter 7, Jesus says it is the heart that has fallen, the heart is corrupt. God doesn't send good people to hell because no one is good.

History also supports this theological claim. G.K. Chesterton once said that original sin, the brokenness of mankind, is the one doctrine that can be proven outside of the Bible, and I think he's right. All we have to do is look at the history of mankind, and it's clear that something is desperately broken with human beings.

paragraphs.heading: What Dr. Jones found
paragraphs.text: A colleague of mine, Dr. Clay Jones, has studied human evil and suffering as much as anybody who's alive. To avoid the claim his critics would make, that he took the easy way out, he decided to study evil in depth in the 20th century. He began with the assumption that evil was done by just a few deranged individuals, but what he found stunned him. What he found was that it wasn't just the Pol Pots and the Hitlers who contributed to evil, but masses of human beings, under the right circumstances and at the right times, did and practiced great acts of evil. What he found was that human beings are deeply wicked.

Let's look at just a few examples from the 20th century. Take the Chinese government, for example, responsible for at least the deaths of 25 to 30 million people. Take the Russians, responsible for starving out at least 6 million Ukrainians. And the Japanese government brutalized at least 300,000 Chinese in what's called the Rape of Nanjing, in a way that even Nazis looking on were horrified. Let's face it, in American culture, tens of millions of abortions and even the practice of eugenics.

The point is that mass evil is not done by individuals. But what Dr. Jones found, I think, is right. Human beings are desperately corrupt. We are deeply fallen. God doesn't send good people to hell, because nobody is truly good. When evil things happen, we often hear people describe it as inhumane. My father taught me when I was younger. He'd say, son, don't describe acts like that as inhumane, because inhumane means not human. He'd say, son, it's humans who do that. And he's right. Whether we turn on the daily news or we look throughout the history of the world, it's human beings who have done and continue to do evil things.

paragraphs.heading: People choose it
paragraphs.text: You might be thinking, okay, okay, so nobody is truly good, but why would God send anybody to hell? Part of the answer is that God doesn't send people to hell. If C.S. Lewis was right in his classic book The Great Divorce, God doesn't send people to hell. People choose it. In fact, toward the end of that book he famously says that in the end there are two kinds of people: those who say to God, thy will be done, and those to whom God says, thy will be done. All who are in hell choose it.

I have a good friend who's clinging to a particular sin in his life, and I'll never forget when he once told me that he would not stop practicing this sin, even if it meant that God would condemn him to hell for eternity. There's a well-known atheist who died recently, and he passed around news for everybody shortly before his death. He said, if any story comes out after I die that I converted on my bedside, that story is false. I will not believe in God. Friends, human autonomy is strong. God has given us free will, and we are stubborn. Many of us don't want to believe in God and all that it entails to follow after him. But you know what? God is a respecter of persons. If people choose not to believe in God, God is not going to force them to believe in him.

paragraphs.heading: Hell brings God no pleasure
paragraphs.text: Please realize, the existence of hell brings no pleasure to God. Medieval depictions of people being tortured mercilessly and endlessly, and somehow God reveling in this with pleasure, are false. Hell is a terrible place. We have been designed to be in a relationship with God and in relationship with other people, and in hell all of that is lost. But in Ezekiel 18 verse 23, God asks this. He says, do I have any pleasure in the death of the wicked? Would I not rather that they turn from their wicked ways and live?

paragraphs.heading: Why can't God just forgive?
paragraphs.text: You might be wondering, well, why can't God just forgive? If God can do anything, can't he just announce that we're forgiven? Well, yes, God can do anything, but he can do anything consistent with his moral nature. God is the holy, righteous judge of the universe, and therefore he can't be indifferent to sin. But what God has done is even better. You see, he's offered the death of his son Jesus Christ, who lived a perfect, sinless life, as an act of love toward us, but also as an act of justice. So the question is, are we willing to accept the free offer of salvation, the free offer of forgiveness, that God has to offer to each one of us?

paragraphs.heading: One compelling reason
paragraphs.text: Let's face it, hell is a troubling thought. I don't like the idea of hell. The thought that some of my friends or family, loved ones, or really anybody could end up in hell is a disturbing thought. When it's all said and done, to me there's one compelling reason to believe that hell is real: Jesus taught about the reality of hell. And Jesus had the most authority and clarity of vision of anybody who's ever lived. As the sinless son of God, who performed miracles and rose from the grave, Jesus had the authority to teach about hell. If Jesus was willing to talk about it and warn people lovingly about the possibility of hell, how could we do any differently?

paragraphs.heading: Stories around the campfire
paragraphs.text: There's nothing like a good campfire: the sound, the smells, and the s'mores. But perhaps what's most special about a campfire are the stories that people tell. I mean, hearing people's stories and listening to others is one of the best ways to build relationships. Since you're here with me at this campfire, let me share a couple of personal stories with you.

paragraphs.heading: A conference I did not expect
paragraphs.text: Not too long ago I went to a national conference that was a part of a movement designed to change the church's view of same-sex relationships. I went there not to rain on anybody's party, but to understand what this movement was about, and just to meet people personally, kind of from the inside. Well, it was like any other conference that I'd been to. There was worship, there were testimonies, but there were also 90-minute sessions where the leaders went into depth on some of the biblical passages, arguing that the church has been wrong about same-sex relationships for 2,000 years. But when they were done, the head person got up there and said, we've assigned each of you at this conference to go to a small classroom, and now you're going to role-play the talking points that you've learned, so you can go back and have conversations with people when you get back home.

Well, we went to these small classrooms, and there's maybe 15 or 20 people there. I sat down, kind of in the shape of a U, like two rows facing up at the front board, and the lady went to the front and she said, we're going to practice these talking points, but before doing so I think it'd be great if each person went around in the room and shared why you're here at this conference and why you're so passionate about this movement. I remember sitting there thinking, I didn't sign up for this. What do I say? What would you say if you were in that same situation? Now, I disagreed with the other people in the room, but some of the stories were heartbreaking, about people who came out to their parents and were kicked out of their home.

And so finally they came to me, and I said, hi, my name is Sean McDowell and I teach at Biola University. And they kind of look at me. I said, well, if you know Biola, you know that I'm probably not theologically where you'd want me to be, but I want to read you something. They had passed out to everybody at the conference, which had about three or four hundred people, these packets, and on the front it said something to the effect of, you are welcome here, you are loved and accepted here. No matter where you are on your journey, you are loved here. And I read it to them. I said, does this apply to me?

paragraphs.heading: We have a lot in common
paragraphs.text: I said, you know, I'm not here to rain on anybody's party. You and I actually have a lot in common. We believe that what Jesus said about the issue of sexuality and relationships is important. We believe what the Bible says about this is important. Although we differ over some of the particulars, you and I actually have a lot in common. But I want you to know something. The narrative is that people like me, who believe the traditional view about sexuality, are hateful, bigoted and homophobic. I just want you to know that that's not always true. In fact, I care about and love each one of you that are in this room.

paragraphs.heading: Truth spoken with grace
paragraphs.text: The reality is that today we find ourselves in these difficult situations where we feel the tension between speaking truth and acting in love. My guess is you've probably found yourself in a similar situation. But remember what Jesus always did: he always spoke truth. He never compromised what was true, because he knew it was the truth that would set people free. But he always spoke that truth with graciousness and with love.

paragraphs.heading: A time when I blew it
paragraphs.text: In contrast to this first story, let me tell you about a time when I blew it. My senior year in college I took a class on apologetics. I was ready and anxious to have a conversation with anybody who wanted to talk with me about spiritual things. Well, shortly after graduation I was up in the mountains and I went to get my hair cut, and as I sat down in the shop I was holding a book that dealt with spiritual issues. The lady who was going to cut my hair was maybe 25 or 30 years old, and I remember she said to me, she goes, oh, is that a book on spiritual issues? Do you mind if I ask you some questions? And I remember thinking, yes. I just took a class on apologetics. Bring it on. I'm ready with an answer.

So I sit down, and she says to me, you know, I've always wondered, if God is so good and powerful, how can there be so much evil and suffering in the world? And instantly I remember thinking, that's all you got? This is easy. So I launched into it. I said, you know, your question about evil assumes there's good, and if there's good, there must be a God. I said, besides, God doesn't want us to be robots. I gave the free will defense. She had another question. I was ready with a response. In my mind, things were going fantastic, until all of a sudden she steps back. She starts to cry and she says, you have an answer for everything. It can't be this simple. And it kind of made me nervous, to be honest, because she's shaking and she's holding scissors to my head. So I changed the subject, gave her a big tip, and we left.

We go walking outside, and I said to my friend who was there with me, man, what's up with her? We're having a great conversation and she starts to cry. And he stops and looks at me right in the eyes and he says, Sean, do you have any idea how arrogant you were toward her? And friends, it hit me like a ton of bricks, and I realized that I was far more concerned with winning an argument, far more concerned with sounding smart, than with really loving her and treating her as a human being. That was one of the first times in my life that my eyes were really opened. I realized that if I have all the answers and I have truth, but I don't have love, I have nothing.

paragraphs.heading: Speaking the truth in love
paragraphs.text: This lesson is not really about the biblical position on homosexuality, or solving the problem of evil. It's not really about any particular issue at all. Rather, it's about speaking the truth in love. As followers of Christ, we need to have the courage to speak truth and to speak it boldly, but not arrogantly, as I did to the lady who was cutting my hair. Do it out of compassion. Do it with a heart of graciousness and kindness toward those who need the truth to set them free.

paragraphs.heading: The unmerciful servant
paragraphs.text: In Matthew 18:21-35, Jesus tells the story of the unmerciful servant. Here is a servant who was forgiven a massive sum from the king, but then he turns around and demands that another servant, who owes him just a few dollars, pay him back. Now, why was this servant so demanding and didn't show forgiveness to the other servant? It's because he failed to truly understand and appreciate how much the king had forgiven him.

I think sometimes we fail to really show grace and love to other people because we don't really understand the depth of sin in our own hearts, and don't understand how much God has forgiven us. If we really want to be able to love people the way God wants us to love them, it begins by first understanding how much God has loved us. If you are willing to speak truth boldly, but do it from a heart motivated by love, and if you're willing to listen to other people's stories because you care about them, and also willing to share yours, I really believe that God could use you to do powerful things within your generation.

paragraphs.heading: Where we take our questions
paragraphs.text: We go to places like Google, YouTube and other search engines regularly to find answers to questions like, where's a good restaurant to eat at? How do you fix a bike? And to track down the most recent gossip on a popular celebrity. But an important question is, why do we go there with our questions? I think the answer is because we believe, at least generally, that we'll find helpful, reliable answers to our questions. In 1 Peter 3:15, the Apostle Peter says to sanctify Christ as Lord in our hearts, to always be ready with an answer for the hope within, and to give it with gentleness and give it with respect.

paragraphs.heading: A life that invites questions
paragraphs.text: Here's a question that's important for us to think about. What would it take for you and me to live the kind of life that would invite questions from other people? How do we live our lives in a certain way where others want to know the source of our hope? And what are some questions we can ask other people to help them along their spiritual journeys?

A few years ago I co-wrote a book called Is God Just a Human Invention with a friend of mine named Jonathan Morrow. The goal was to provide succinct and yet thoughtful answers to the 17 biggest questions skeptics and atheists were asking about God.

paragraphs.heading: Sitting in the hot seat
paragraphs.text: While Christians were reading it I was getting a good response, but I started to think to myself, how could I get other non-believers to read it and engage with the ideas? So I called up one of the largest skeptic groups near where I live. I told the head of it, I said, I'd be happy to come sit in the hot seat of your group and just answer questions that you and some of the other skeptics in your group would have toward a Christian. I went up there and they had questions about the existence of God, questions about the Bible, political questions, and even specific questions about what I believed about the soul. It was a blast.

Before the event began, I'd asked the leader if it was okay, toward the end, if I could ask them some questions. Now, I could have asked this group of skeptics how they explain the origin of information in DNA, or the origin of the universe, or how they explain the evidence for the resurrection of Jesus. While those are great questions, I decided to take a different approach. Instead, I asked questions like: what blind spots do Christians have? What bad impressions do Christians often leave? And how can Christians improve their interaction with skeptics?

paragraphs.heading: What the skeptics said
paragraphs.text: And I'll never forget a lady sitting right in the front to my right. She was maybe 70 years old. She said, listen. I said, tell me what you mean. She said, a lot of my Christian friends want to speak to me, tell me why I'm wrong, preach the gospel at me, occasionally tell me I'm going to hell. But when I want to share my beliefs, they don't want to listen to me. Why should I listen to them when they don't listen to me?

The fellow in the back, who's maybe 50 years old and who described himself as a former Christian, he said, stop slandering atheists. And I said, well, that's a pretty serious charge, what do you mean? He said, look, I'm an atheist, but occasionally I'll just show up and I'll go to church. People don't know who I am or why I'm there. I just listen. He said almost every time I show up I hear some cheap shot, often from the stage, about atheists or some other non-Christian group. Here's the bottom line: if we don't treat non-believers the way that Christ calls us to, they so often won't even hear what we believe is true.

paragraphs.heading: Grace and truth
paragraphs.text: You see, the Bible tells us that Jesus came in grace and he came in truth. He came in grace, which is in a loving relationship, and he also spoke truth. We are called to speak truth. We can't compromise truth, but we must do it in love. If we mess up the relationship, so often people won't even hear what we believe is true. If we want people to ask us questions about our faith, we need to be living the kind of lives that invite inquiry. We need to be living the kind of lives that make people wonder, what is the source of that person's hope? But we also need to be ready with some thoughtful questions we can ask other people to help them along on their spiritual journeys.

paragraphs.heading: Four questions worth asking
paragraphs.text: Here are some specific questions that I've found helpful in my own experience and relationships. First, what do you believe? It's important to find out what the other person believes. Proverbs 18:13 says it is foolish and shameful to answer before you hear. To have an honest conversation with somebody, we first have to understand what that person really believes, and that person is only going to share what they believe when we ask good questions and really listen. Second, why do you believe it?

What reasons does the person have for his or her beliefs? Proverbs 20 verse 5 says that the purpose in a man's heart is like deep water, but it takes a person of understanding who can draw it out. In other words, people have deep reasons for why they believe as they do, and sometimes people know those reasons and sometimes they don't.

Take my father, for example. Before he became a Christian he was an angry agnostic. He looked for ways to shoot Christians down and prove that they were wrong. One thing he didn't fully realize at the time is that he would hear people talk about a Heavenly Father and he thought, why would I want a Heavenly Father? That idea turned him off. Why? Because his earthly father was abusive and absent. His relationship with his father was a deep reason that gave him some anger against God. People have deep reasons for why they believe as they do, and it takes wisdom and listening and patience to help draw out what those real reasons often are.

The third question is, where do we agree? Where can we find common ground? Finding common ground is a powerful way to have meaningful spiritual conversations with other people. When we find common ground, often someone's guard will go down and they'll listen in a way they wouldn't have listened before. When I was meeting with these skeptics, they were surprised to find out, even though we clearly differ on a number of significant issues, how much we actually have in common.

And the fourth question is, where do we disagree? I've had at least two significant spiritual conversations with skeptics about the origin of the universe, and in each of these conversations we talked about the science and the philosophy that points toward the universe having a beginning. As we got back to really the basis of the argument, I said to him, either you have to believe that the universe can come into existence from nothing, or you believe there's a cause outside of space, outside of time, that speaks the universe into existence. Which do you find more reasonable? And both of them looked me right in the eyes and said, a universe from nothing is most reasonable.

Now, in some ways I'm not exactly sure where to take the argument from that, so I just said back to him, okay, here's where you and I differ. I think it's more reasonable that there's a God who speaks the universe into existence. You think it's more reasonable that something can come from nothing. All I was trying to do was clarify the cost of being an atheist. Now, interestingly, in a matter of time one of them actually became a believer. In my experience, most people are willing to have genuine spiritual conversations. If we treat people the way they want to be treated, they'll often return the favor to us. If we really listen to people and value their opinions, most people will listen back and value what we have to say as well.

paragraphs.heading: You are ready
paragraphs.text: You have learned some powerful lessons in this study, and you are ready for spiritual conversations. Now, I don't think you have to have all the answers. I don't have even close to all the answers. If someone asks you a tough question, just simply say, I don't know, and then go find an answer so you'll know next time. If you're willing to ask good questions, listen to people and stick with people through their journeys, I think you'll be amazed at how God will use you in people's lives to make a difference with them spiritually. Go for it.

paragraphs.heading: Questions in my upper teens
paragraphs.text: Since I grew up in a Christian home, the Christian story always made sense to me. My parents have worked their entire lives with a professional Christian ministry. My dad has spent his life writing, speaking and debating the truth of the Christian message. Yet when I was in my upper teens, I had some questions that kind of troubled me, that seemed more pertinent in my life than ever before. Questions like, how do I really know that Christianity is true? What if I was born in a different family or in a different culture, would I still believe the Christian message? What if my beliefs are false?

paragraphs.heading: Telling my dad
paragraphs.text: I decided it was time to share my doubts and my questions with my father, not knowing how he would respond. After all, he spent his life teaching the Christian message to others. We were up in the mountains at a small coffee shop, and I remember leaning in to my dad and saying, Dad, I want to know what's true, but I don't know that I'm convinced that Christianity is true. And he instantly looked right back at me. He goes, son, I think that's great. And for a second I said, wait a minute, Dad, did you hear what I just said? I'm doubting Christianity. And he said, I did hear you, son, and I think this is good.

Because you can't live your life based on my convictions. You have to come to a point where you know and believe that Christianity is true for yourself. He said, don't rebel just for the sake of rebelling. So many young people growing up reject what their parents taught them just out of spite. He said, if you walk away, only do so because you're convinced that Christianity is not true. And no matter what you decide, you need to know that your mom and I will always love you.

paragraphs.heading: Unexpressed doubts
paragraphs.text: Doubts and questions are not bad. Whenever my students come up to me and say, hey, Mr. McDowell, I've got some questions and doubts, I always respond by saying, that's fantastic, I'm so glad you're asking these questions. Now, that's not the typical response that they expect, because sometimes we think that asking questions and doubting God and his Word can be bad. But that's not always the case. You see, doubts can be good if we see them as opportunities to go deeper in our faith. It's not doubts that are bad, it's unexpressed doubts that can be bad. You see, it's not doubts that are corrosive to faith. It's when we have doubts and we don't seek answers. So if you have doubts about your faith, the first thing to do is to just share them with somebody and start the conversation.

paragraphs.heading: Where a doubt really comes from
paragraphs.text: There are a variety of reasons that might motivate someone to have questions and doubts. Some can certainly be intellectual, but I'm convinced that more often than not the source of a doubt, the heart of a doubt, comes from emotional, relational or moral reasons. Consider a couple of stories that might help.

First, I met a young man while speaking at a conference in Chicago, and when I was done he came up to me and said, hey, can we go outside and talk a little further? I've got some questions for you, some doubts about my faith. I said, sure. So we went outside, and he had some questions about whether Jesus could really be God. He had questions about other religions. And after doing my best to answer his questions, I sensed that something deeper was going on. I said something to the effect of, you know, I'm answering your questions, but I think something else is going on with you. What is it?

And essentially it came out. He admitted it. He said, you know what, I was raised in the Christian faith, but I'm just about to graduate from high school, I'm heading to college, and I've joined a fraternity. I just want to have some fun. And then it hit me. Although he raised intellectual questions and challenges to the faith, that wasn't the heart of his doubt. The heart of his doubts were moral. He wanted to live a certain way, and saw his Christian beliefs as getting in the way of what he thought would be the most fun.

paragraphs.heading: Relationships and how we see God
paragraphs.text: Second, our relationships can deeply affect the way we relate to God. Take my father, for example. He had a distant and a drunk father, so he would hear people say things like, hey, you have a Heavenly Father who loves you, and my dad would think, wait a minute, father equals hurt and distance and pain. Why would I want a Heavenly Father when it just brings more pain? You see, the reality is our relationships, especially our broken relationships, can drive questions and doubts about God. An important question we really need to ask ourselves is, how have our relationships, the ones that have been good and the ones that have failed, affected the way we view and relate to God?

People who go through doubts will often describe it as if the ground is crumbling beneath them, or they're fumbling around in the dark. The experience of doubts can be very painful and can bring up a lot of fears. That's why one of the places to begin is to really identify what's at the heart, what's at the source of my doubts. And this requires a lot of searching.

paragraphs.heading: John the Baptist's doubt
paragraphs.text: Surprisingly, one of the most prominent examples of doubt in the Bible comes from John the Baptist, the prophesied forerunner of Christ the Messiah. Herod had John the Baptist arrested and thrown in prison, and he sends his disciples to Jesus to ask him, are you the one, or should we expect another? Well, the question is, why did John the Baptist have questions and doubts at this point in his life? And the answer is because he was alone and he was suffering. Loneliness and pain are common reasons why people have questions and doubts about God.

Jesus's response is powerful. He doesn't scold John. He doesn't chastise him. He doesn't show disappointment in John for having questions and doubts. Rather, he gives John evidence. In Luke 7:22 through 23, it describes how Jesus says to his disciples, go back and tell John what you have seen and what you have heard. The deaf hear, the blind see, the lame walk, and the dead live again, and the poor have the good news preached to them.

So what does this tell us? Well, for one thing, it tells us that doubts are a normal and natural part of life. All of us should expect to have questions at some point in our journey of faith. In fact, even the apostles had doubts. It says in Matthew 28 that they worshiped Jesus as God, and yet some of them doubted. Can you imagine that? The very people who saw the risen Jesus had doubts. If John the Baptist and the apostles had doubts, you better believe that some of us, if not most of us, will have doubts at some point in our life. That's why I believe that Jude 22 says to have mercy on those who doubt.

paragraphs.heading: Doubt is not the opposite of faith
paragraphs.text: Doubt is not the opposite of faith. In fact, doubt can often serve as the basis for developing a more robust faith. The key is to identify what is the source of the doubt. If your doubts are emotional, you might need to find and experience some emotional healing. If your doubts are relational, you might need to restore some broken relationships. And if your doubts are intellectual, you need to find some answers to your questions. You see, doubt is not necessarily corrosive to faith, but can be the opportunity to develop a deeper and a lasting faith.

paragraphs.heading: A friend with a way out
paragraphs.text: Years ago our family became friends with another young family in our neighborhood. The kids were about the same age as our kids, and the mom and dad had a lot in common with my wife and I. Well, as we got to know him, it was very clear that the father, who became a good friend of mine, was not a Christian. In fact, we had conversations about heaven and hell. We had conversations about the scientific evidence for God, and he was the consummate skeptic. He always had a way out, or a question, or a way of avoiding the evidence. And then years later they ended up moving to the Northwest.

When I heard that they were going to move, I had a couple of thoughts. I thought, well, number one, gosh, he's no longer going to have me in his life, and other Christian friends in our neighborhood, to talk to him about God. And he's such a skeptic, he's never going to believe. But then sometime later I started noticing he was posting quotes by C.S. Lewis on social media. He was posting these Christian ideas. To make a long story short, a few summers ago I had a chance to go up to the Northwest and baptize him, because he'd become a Christian. And on that same day his young son was baptized as well. It was truly one of the most amazing experiences of my life.

paragraphs.heading: Four principles
paragraphs.text: I think there's four principles we can learn from this experience. First, for many people, coming to faith can take a long time, sometimes even years. Many people have emotional, intellectual, moral and relational issues to work through, and this is certainly true for my friend, before they can consider the claims of Christ. Second, sometimes people are at a point in their lives where they're just not open to faith. Even people walked away from Jesus in the flesh.

Years ago, when my friend was still a skeptic, I had him speak into a group of my high school students, and I was trying to teach my students, how do you have genuine conversations with people who see the world differently? And in the middle of this conversation, my friend said to my students, look, if your teacher Sean could give me evidence, I would believe. I just don't see the evidence. And then in the conversation later, somehow it shifted. I don't remember how, but somehow the group was talking about the legalization of marijuana, and my friend says, he goes, look, the bottom line is I just don't want the government coming into my house telling me how to live. It's my house.

paragraphs.heading: It was never the evidence
paragraphs.text: And I stopped him. I said, wait a minute, a minute ago you said you'd follow the evidence. Now I think you have the answer why you don't. You know, Jesus says, I stand at the door and knock. He's the ultimate governing authority. God wants to come into your house and tell you how to live. You didn't want the government to tell you whether you could smoke marijuana or not. Maybe the real issue is you just don't want God in your life telling you how to live. He looked at me and he says, I don't understand. I tried three times to explain it, and I gave up. Do you know that years later, when he became a Christian, he pointed back to that, and he said, Sean, you were right. It wasn't a lack of evidence. I simply did not want an authority in my life telling me how to live. Friends, sometimes people are not at a point in their life, for a variety of reasons, to even be open to issues of faith.

Third, my friend shared with me that back when he was a skeptic, he had doubts about his faith. Now, we just talked about doubt, and sometimes we tend to think that it's only Christians who have doubts, but that's not true. People of all walks of life and different beliefs often have doubts. My friend would go to sleep at night sometimes and wonder, is there really anything to this claim about God? What if I'm wrong about my skeptical beliefs? So the challenge for us is to ask the right questions to get people to doubt their skeptical beliefs and hopefully come to Christ.

paragraphs.heading: Relationships really matter
paragraphs.text: And fourth, relationships really matter. It was certainly truth that was important in my friend's journey, but it was also the love and relationship of believers that drew him in when his heart was open. We've talked a lot in this study about how important it is to speak truth, but to do it in a loving fashion. Jesus came in grace and he came in truth. Yes, we need to speak truth, but from a heart of love and a heart of compassion. In fact, we need to be willing to love people because they're made in the image of God, even if they never come to faith.

paragraphs.heading: The journey we have taken
paragraphs.text: We have been on a long journey together. We started by looking at the relationship between faith and reason and exploring questions of truth. Then we looked at some different worldviews: pantheism, naturalism and monotheism. Then we considered the scientific evidence from DNA and fine-tuning, pointing toward an intelligent designer. And then after that, we looked at these signposts that point toward purpose in the universe: beauty, morality, free will and story. Then we examined the specific historical evidence for Jesus and for the reliability of the Bible. And then after that we considered some of the biggest objections to the faith, hell and evil.

paragraphs.heading: You are ready
paragraphs.text: And in this final unit we've asked the question, what now? Do you have all your questions answered? Probably not. In fact, you might even have more questions now than when we started. But I want to impress something very important upon you, and it's this: that you are ready. You've been trained well. I had a public debate some years ago, and I called up one of my professors from grad school, and as we were talking about it he said something to me I'll never forget. He said, Sean, you've been trained well. And the same is true for you. You will always have questions. There's always new issues that arise. But you have learned truth well, and you are ready, if you put your training into practice, to engage family and friends and others of our non-believing world with the gospel.

You're ready. Not only are you ready, but God wants you to step out boldly and put this training into practice. You maybe have heard it said that with great power comes great responsibility. This is actually a biblical idea. Jesus said, he who has been given much, much is required. You've been blessed by people who care enough about you to take you through this training. The question is, what will you do with it? God wants you to speak truth boldly, and yet he wants you to do it with a heart of love. He wants you to speak truth with compassion.

paragraphs.heading: Will that be you?
paragraphs.text: Friends, we live in a broken and a hurting world that desperately needs Jesus. We live in a world that desperately needs people to speak the truth about Jesus, the only truth that can set people free. The question is, will that be you?
